deeper_properties: When only even bottom numbers $0$, $2$, $4$ up to $2020$ appear, flipping signs need a square that is negative. Since $(\sqrt{3})^2$ equals $3$ is positive, all signs would stay plus, while $(i\sqrt{3})^2$ equals $-3$ is negative, so its even powers go $1$, $-3$, $9$ and the sign flips each time.

In $(1+i\sqrt{3})^{2020}$ multiplied out, every term with an odd power still contains one $i$. Keeping only the part without $i$ throws exactly those away, which is why the statement shows only even bottom numbers.

candidates.name: Even part of $(1+x)^{2020}$ with $x^2=-3$ by distance and angle
candidates.from_first_principles: The middle terms give the pattern and the last term confirms it: term number $k$ is $C(2020,2k)$ times $(-3)^k$. Since $(i\sqrt{3})^2$ equals $-3$, which is negative, that is $C(2020,2k)$ times $(i\sqrt{3})^{2k}$, exactly the even-power terms when $(1+i\sqrt{3})^{2020}$ is multiplied out. Adding the same bracket with $-i\sqrt{3}$ cancels the odd-power terms, which still contain $i$, and leaves twice the sum, so the sum is half that pair. De Moivre's theorem, raising a complex number to a power raises its distance from zero to that power and multiplies its angle by it, then replaces $2020$ multiplications by one distance and one angle, and the final angle decides how much of that distance the part without $i$ keeps, sign included.
candidates.why: It wins because every step comes from the statement: the first terms give the pattern, the last term confirms the sign, and the promise of a single power is what the distance-and-angle picture delivers.
